blocks.html: A numeric variable, measured on an interval or ratio scale (recall §1.1.2), usually has too many distinct values to give each its own bar. The charts in this section therefore start from the grouped frequency distribution (recall §1.4.2) or from the quartiles (recall §3.3). They show the distribution’s shape, centre and spread: the histogram (§4.3.1), the frequency polygon (§4.3.2), the ogive (§4.3.3), the box plot (§4.3.4) and the stem-and-leaf plot (§4.3.5).
Histogram

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A histogram draws each class interval of a grouped frequency distribution as a bar on a continuous numeric axis, with adjoining bars and no gaps between them, and with bar area proportional to the class frequency. With equal class widths, bar height is proportional to frequency too.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Take the grouped weights of today’s 30 clinic children (recall §1.4.1): 8 to <10 kg, 5 children; 10 to <12 kg, 12; 12 to <14 kg, 9; 14 to <16 kg, 4. Draw each class as a bar from its lower to its upper boundary. The bars touch because weight flows continuously from one class into the next; there is no real gap between 9.99 kg and 10.00 kg. The CDC describes the histogram as using “adjoining columns” for the class intervals (CDC, 2012b).

blocks.caption: Figure 4.4. Histogram of the weights of today’s 30 clinic children, classes 8 to <10, 10 to <12, 12 to <14 and 14 to <16 kg.

blocks.html: The histogram peaks in the 10 to <12 kg class and is only mildly asymmetric, consistent with the small Pearson skewness of today’s weights (recall §3.9).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Suppose you merged the last two classes into one class, 12 to <16 kg, with 9 + 4 = 13 children.

  1. If you drew its bar at height 13, it would stand taller than the 10 to <12 kg bar (12) and be twice as wide, so it would look far more crowded.
  2. Use frequency density instead: frequency ÷ class width. For 12 to <16 kg: 13 ÷ 4 = 3.25 children per kg.
  3. Compare: 8 to <10 kg, 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 per kg; 10 to <12 kg, 12 ÷ 2 = 6.0 per kg.
  4. Result: drawn at height 3.25, the merged bar has area 3.25 × 4 = 13, the right share, and correctly shows the 12 to <16 kg range as about half as crowded per kg as 10 to <12 kg.

points.html: Adjoining bars on a continuous axis distinguish a histogram from a bar diagram.
With unequal class widths, plot frequency density so that area, not height, carries the frequency.

The histogram is the quickest informal look at skewness (recall §3.9) and at whether a variable looks roughly bell-shaped, before you use the Normal distribution (§5.7.2.2) or formal tests of normality (§9.3).
The number of classes changes the picture: too few hides detail, too many shows noise (recall Sturges’ rule, §1.4.1).

blocks.html: Frequency Polygon

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A frequency polygon plots each class frequency at the class mid-point and joins the points with straight lines. It is closed by adding a point of zero frequency one class width beyond each end.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Put a dot at the top-centre of each histogram bar and join the dots. The polygon shows the same shape as the histogram, as an outline rather than blocks. It is not smoothed: the lines are straight segments between mid-points. Its practical use is comparison: two polygons, for example urban and rural clinic weights, can share one set of axes, where two overlapping histograms would be cluttered.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html: With equal class widths h, the closed polygon has exactly the same area as the histogram. Take any segment joining two adjacent mid-points. At the class boundary halfway between them, the segment cuts a small triangle off the corner of one bar and adds a triangle of the same base (h/2) and the same height to the neighbouring region. The two triangles are congruent, so the area lost equals the area gained. The two closing segments do the same at each end: the triangle added outside the first class equals the triangle cut from its corner. Summing over all segments, polygon area = histogram area = h × N. The CDC states the same result: a frequency polygon “contains the same area under the line as does a histogram of the same data” (CDC, 2012b).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Histogram area = Σ f × h = (5 + 12 + 9 + 4) × 2 = 60 child-kg.
  2. Polygon points: (7, 0), (9, 5), (11, 12), (13, 9), (15, 4), (17, 0).
  3. Area by trapezoids, each of width 2: 2 × [(0 + 5)/2 + (5 + 12)/2 + (12 + 9)/2 + (9 + 4)/2 + (4 + 0)/2] = 2 × (2.5 + 8.5 + 10.5 + 6.5 + 2.0) = 2 × 30 = 60 child-kg.
  4. Result: the two areas are equal, as the derivation predicts.

blocks.alt: Frequency polygon over the same weight data
blocks.caption: Figure 4.5. Frequency polygon (line) over the histogram of today’s 30 weights (shaded). Both enclose 60 child-kg.

points.html: The polygon uses the same mid-points and frequencies as the histogram. It is a redrawing of the same data, not new data.

As the classes narrow and the number of observations grows, the polygon drawn on the frequency-density scale (recall §4.3.1), with total area rescaled to 1, approaches a smooth curve. That is the idea behind the probability density curve of a continuous random variable (§5.6.2, a curve whose area over an interval gives a probability).

blocks.html: Ogive

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: An ogive is a cumulative frequency curve. The usual “less than” ogive plots the cumulative frequency (or cumulative percentage) against the upper boundary of each class. A “more than” ogive plots the number of observations at or above each lower class boundary.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Cumulative frequency is a running total (recall §1.4.3); the ogive draws that running total as a line. Because a running total can only grow or stay the same, the “less than” ogive never falls. It is usually S-shaped: steep where the data are dense, flat in the tails. The “more than” ogive is its mirror image and never rises.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: For today’s 30 weights, the “less than” ogive passes through (8, 0), (10, 5), (12, 17), (14, 26), (16, 30). The “more than” ogive passes through (8, 30), (10, 25), (12, 13), (14, 4), (16, 0).

blocks.caption: Figure 4.6. “Less than” and “more than” ogives for today’s 30 weights. They cross at a cumulative count of 15 (N/2), above the median.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Read the median from the ogive.

  1. The median is the value with N/2 = 30/2 = 15 children below it.
  2. On the “less than” ogive, 15 lies between (10, 5) and (12, 17).
  3. Interpolate along the straight segment: 10 + (15 − 5) ÷ (17 − 5) × 2 = 10 + 10/12 × 2 = 11.67 kg.
  4. Check with the “more than” ogive: on the segment from (10, 25) to (12, 13), the count 15 is reached at 10 + (25 − 15) ÷ (25 − 13) × 2 = 11.67 kg. The two curves cross there.
  5. Result: graphical median = 11.67 kg, the same value as the grouped-data median formula of §2.3. The median of the 30 raw weights is 11.7 kg; grouping costs very little here.

points.html: Any percentile can be read the same way: find the cumulative count (or percentage) on the y-axis, go across to the curve, then down to the x-axis.
The “less than” and “more than” ogives always cross at the median, because at that point the counts below and above are both N/2.
Joining the plotted points with straight lines is the same assumption the grouped-median formula makes: values are spread evenly within each class.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 4.2

questions.prompt: Name the one visual feature that tells you at once whether you are looking at a histogram or a bar diagram, and say why that feature exists.
questions.answer: Histogram bars adjoin, with no gaps, because the x-axis is a continuous numeric scale and one class runs straight into the next. Bar-diagram bars stand apart, because each bar is a separate category (ordered or not) with nothing in between.

questions.prompt: Using the “less than” ogive points for today’s 30 weights, estimate the first quartile (the weight with 7.5 children below it).
questions.answer: The count 7.5 lies between the points (10, 5) and (12, 17). Interpolating: Q1 ≈ 10 + (7.5 − 5) ÷ (17 − 5) × 2 = 10 + 2.5/12 × 2 = 10.42 kg. (The Q1 of the 30 raw weights by R’s default method is 10.57 kg; the ogive estimate assumes values are spread evenly within the class.)

questions.prompt: A histogram of haemoglobin uses classes 7 to <9, 9 to <11 and 11 to <15 g/dL, with 10, 30 and 40 women. What height should each bar have, and which class is the most crowded per g/dL?
questions.answer: The widths are unequal (2, 2 and 4 g/dL), so plot frequency density = frequency ÷ width: 10 ÷ 2 = 5, 30 ÷ 2 = 15 and 40 ÷ 4 = 10 women per g/dL. The 9 to <11 g/dL class is the most crowded (15 per g/dL), even though the 11 to <15 class holds the most women. Drawn at height 40, the last bar would wrongly look the densest.

blocks.note: (Answers in the Appendix at the end of the book.)

blocks.html: Box Plot

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A box plot draws a box from the first quartile (Q1) to the third quartile (Q3), with a line at the median, and whiskers out from the box. Two versions are in use:

  • Five-number-summary box plot: whiskers run to the minimum and the maximum.
  • Tukey box plot (R’s default box plot): compute the fences Q1 − 1.5 × IQR and Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. Each whisker runs to the most extreme observation that lies inside its fence, and every observation beyond a fence is plotted as a separate point, a potential outlier. The whisker ends at a data value, not at the fence itself.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The box is the IQR, the middle 50% of the data (recall §3.4); the line inside it is the median; the whiskers show how far the rest of the data reach. The box plot was introduced by John Tukey as part of exploratory data analysis. Variants exist: some use other multipliers than 1.5, some draw whiskers to fixed percentiles, and software differs in how it computes quartiles (Wickham & Stryjewski, 2011). The 1.5 × IQR rule is therefore a convention, and a figure legend should say which version is drawn.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In the CBHI survey, distance from home to the nearest health facility was recorded for all 500 households (Figure 4.7).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Non-members (n = 350):

  1. Q1 = 6.6 km, median = 8.5 km, Q3 = 10.2 km, so IQR = 10.2 − 6.6 = 3.6 km.
  2. 1.5 × IQR = 5.4 km. Lower fence = 6.6 − 5.4 = 1.2 km; upper fence = 10.2 + 5.4 = 15.6 km.
  3. The maximum, 15.3 km, is inside the upper fence, so the upper whisker ends at 15.3 km.
  4. Fourteen households live less than 1.2 km away (from 0.0 to 1.1 km). They are plotted as separate points. The nearest value inside the fence is 1.3 km, so the lower whisker ends at 1.3 km, not at the fence (1.2 km) and not at the minimum (0.0 km).

Members (n = 150):

  1. Q1 = 3.5 km, median = 6.9 km, Q3 = 9.2 km (9.175 before rounding), so IQR = 5.675 km.
  2. Fences: 3.5 − 8.5 = −5.0 km and 9.175 + 8.5 = 17.7 km. The minimum (0.2 km) and maximum (14.7 km) both lie inside, so the whiskers reach them. For members, the Tukey and five-number box plots are identical.

Result: members tend to live nearer the facility (median 6.9 vs 8.5 km). The non-member distribution is skewed to the left, with a tail of households living next to the facility.

blocks.alt: Box plot of distance to facility by CBHI membership
blocks.caption: Figure 4.7. Tukey box plots of distance to the health facility, CBHI survey (350 non-members, 150 members). Whiskers end at the last observation inside the fences; the 14 points below the non-members’ lower fence are drawn separately.

points.html: The box plot is at its best when it compares one numeric variable across groups on the same axis, for example birthweight across several blocks.

Asymmetry shows skewness without calculation: the median off-centre in the box, or one whisker longer than the other. In Figure 4.7 the non-members’ lower tail, with its 14 outliers, reaches 8.5 km below the median (to 0.0 km), while the upper tail reaches only 6.8 km above it (to 15.3 km): a left skew.

A point beyond a fence is a potential outlier to check against the source records. It is not an error by definition, and it is not deleted for being unusual. In a right-skewed variable such as hospital length of stay, the long stays beyond the upper fence are real and important.

blocks.html: Stem-and-Leaf Plot

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A stem-and-leaf plot splits each value into a stem (the leading digits) and a leaf (the last digit), and lists the leaves beside their stems. It shows the shape of the distribution and keeps every value.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The histogram, frequency polygon, ogive and box plot give up individual values: once a weight goes into a class or a quartile, you cannot read it back. Of the five charts in this section, the stem-and-leaf plot is the only one that keeps every value. Turned on its side, it looks like a histogram. The scatter diagram (§4.4) also keeps every value, but it plots two variables.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Today’s 30 weights, with whole kilograms as the stem and the first decimal as the leaf:

Stem (kg) Leaves (0.1 kg)
8 6
9 1 4 7 8
10 0 3 5 8
11 0 1 2 4 5 6 8 9
12 0 3 4 6 9
13 1 4 6 8
14 1 4 8
15 3

The row lengths (1, 4, 4, 8, 5, 4, 3, 1; total 30) trace the shape, with the peak at 11 kg, and you can still read off every value: the lightest child weighed 8.6 kg and the heaviest 15.3 kg.

points.html: It keeps exact values, so medians and quartiles can be counted straight off the display.
It suits small datasets. With hundreds of values the rows become too long, and a histogram shows the shape more efficiently.
Choose the stem unit so that you get a sensible number of rows, much as you choose class width for a histogram.
